posts.content_md:
Well, I am starting to get the itch again to get back into the lab. Plus my third world basement won't be as cold in a few weeks. I have some H1 transmission masters I want to copy but I don't have a vibration isolation table. 

So, I think I may start exploring the idea of making dedicated holographic camera's for more ellaborate geometries. In other words, set the camera up such that each optic is rigidly fastened to a frame of sorts, such that relative movement of the optics is elliminated. I probably only need about 20 seconds of exposure at max.

Here is a SBR camera I made when I made my first DCG hologram. Only the laser and first transfer mirror is not part of the camera.

posts.author: Justin W
posts.content_md:
Hi John!

If I can ask a few questions about what I see here....

Do I see a (perhaps) 8" parabolic mirror steering your beam to plate/object?

If yes then I'll presume that you are using what becomes at that point a collimated beam for a single-beam reflection (Denisyuk) hologram....

...which goes a long way toward answering one big question I've always had about SBR - is a diverging beam required? Seems not. Very cool.

I've personally not yet had any success shooting SBR... I use VRP-M with a 532nm laser and according to a Slavich website out there somewhere, this is no big surprise with VRP-M (as this emulsion requires high carrier modulation(!?) in order to achieve good diffraction efficiency)..WeverTH *that*means.... I guess I take that to mean that VRP-M likes a strong object beam....

I notice no kicker mirrors pictured in your setup there - would you say that using a collimated single beam results in brighter object illumination than one would see with a diverging beam?

Personal note - I'm powerfully curious lately about getting back to the basics. I've plans for my new table that will someday soon here isolate me from the oh-so-bothersome vibrations of this manic world, and have done enough H1/H2 work now to say I know how to do it (yay), but have also determined that I'll not soon be able to afford large enough film to create masters big enough to get a reasonable viewing range from an H2.. So - back to the basics. I think it's time to get back to off-axis reflection, and maybe even attempt some SBR's ... I bet kicker mirrors are way necessary with VRP-M, even with whatever improvement in beam ratio I may see by going collimated...

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Hey Justin, how's it going?

It is actually a 6" collimator. This was in the beginning for DCG and I was only doing 4x5 plates. So a 6" collimator was plenty for this camera. 

I try to use a collimated beam for SBR if the optics allow. Using a collimated beam allows your SBR to be used as a master for iamge planed proximity copying. 

On a side note, if you don't have a collimator, placing your objective as far away from the plate as possible helps.

I would have to say that, and this is probably only a slight advantage, that using a collimated or better still a converging beam will increase the amount of light slightly to the object resulting in more object light. But I bet it is very slight unless a highly converging beam is used with an object a few inches from the plate. (Man, this is a good thought and one that should be confirmed). Wonder if the trade off is worth it.

No I did not use any kicker mirrors in this set up but YES, YES, YES kicker mirrors definitely help in a SBR.

When you start SBR's in DCG I will point out you can add additional lighting right through the plate. Much easier for those objects that are close to the plate.

Peace!
